title: Conscience
lead: The inner sense of right and wrong that Paul calls syneidesis, 'knowing with oneself'. The Old Testament has no single word for it, though it speaks of the heart that strikes a person (1 Samuel 24:5; 2 Samuel 24:10). In Paul conscience bears witness (Romans 2:15; 9:1), can be weak or wounded (1 Corinthians 8:7-12), and is a reason to submit to rulers (Romans 13:5). The churches have argued over whether conscience is a reliable guide, how far it binds, and who may bind it.

sections.b: The Greek word syneidēsis is the self's awareness of what it has done and whether it was right. It is rare in the Greek Old Testament and in the Gospels, and frequent in Paul. In Romans it appears three times: as the witness in the hearts of Gentiles who do what the law requires (2:15), as Paul's own witness "in the Holy Spirit" (9:1), and as the reason for submitting to authority, "not only to escape the anger, but also for the sake of conscience" (13:5). The related idea of acting from conviction appears in chapter 14: each person should be "fully sure in their own mind" (14:5), and "anything not done out of faith is sin" (14:23). Conscience is a witness, not a final judge, since only the Lord judges (14:4, 10).
sections.refs: Romans 2:15; Romans 9:1; Romans 13:5; Romans 14:5; Romans 14:22-23; 1 Corinthians 8:7

sections.b: Augustine called the unbeliever's virtues weak because they do not come from faith (using Romans 14:23). Aquinas held that a person is bound to follow even an erring conscience. Luther's stand at Worms (1521), that his conscience was captive to the word of God, made conscience a mark of the Reformation. The Westminster Confession (ch. 20) says that God alone is lord of the conscience, and Baptists made liberty of conscience the basis of their case against state churches (Roger Williams, 1644). The Catholic Church teaches that conscience must be formed by the church's teaching and by the moral law (Catechism 1776-1802).
